I'm 66 years old, and I've been farming these plots in Quzhou County since I was a teenager. My family has 8 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. I know every inch of it. At my age, I don't chase new fads — I stick to what works. The wheat–corn rotation has fed my family for generations, and this year will be no different.

My winter wheat went into the ground last October. I'll manage it through to harvest in early June, then immediately plant summer corn — no rest for the land or for me. That's the double-cropping system we live by here. I use improved wheat varieties like the ones from the county seed station; they're reliable and I save some seed each year. For corn, I buy hybrid seed in sealed packages — you can't skimp on hybrid corn, or you lose half your yield. I rotary till before wheat sowing, but after the wheat comes off, I'll plant corn with no-tillage to save time and keep the soil from drying out.

Fertilizer is expensive, but you can't cheat the soil. For wheat, I spread compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea when the wheat joints in spring — total nitrogen around 18 kg per mu. For corn, I put down high-nitrogen compound at planting and maybe a side-dressing of urea if the leaves turn yellow — about 16 kg nitrogen per mu. I irrigate from my well: four times for wheat (winter, green-up, jointing, and filling) and twice for corn (after sowing and at the big-flare stage). I spray pesticides three times per crop — herbicide once, insecticide once or twice, and fungicide if the weather turns damp.

I expect about 500 kg of wheat per mu and 600 kg of corn per mu if the weather holds. It won't make me rich, but it will pay for my grandchildren's school fees and leave enough for our own flour and cooking oil.
